summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct at the national level. Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Section 377D's "gross indecency" offence carries up to two years. Kuala Lumpur stands directly under this Penal Code, with no local ordinance displacing it. The prohibition on sodomy dates to 1871.

Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya also maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them, while the federal Penal Code applies to that visitor in full. All 13 states have passed such enactments since the 1980s, three of them also barring women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is official policy at the capital level. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022; the Human Diguity Trust profile records the same operation as conducted jointly by Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and Jawi at an all-male health centre, with over 200 arrested. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Arrest, prosecution and corporal punishment have all been recorded as enforcement outcomes since the 2018 election. Trans people in Malaysia also face lethal violence and official indifference to it: a transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical exposure is the Penal Code rather than the Sharia layer. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
A Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report of 10 August 2022 documents state-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia, based on interviews with 73 LGBT people conducted between 2018 and 2021, among them residents of Kuala Lumpur. The report states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground. It calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity; no such reform has been enacted.

The Human Dignity Trust profile of Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records the Federal Court's striking down of some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power while the federal offences remain in force, so a visitor assessing the litigation wins should treat them as removing only the layer that does not apply to non-Muslims.
localsOnly:
Sharia cross-dressing offences apply to Muslims only, so they bind Malaysian Muslim residents and Muslim visitors but not non-Muslim tourists. Enforcement is conducted by state Islamic religious departments rather than ordinary police, and the provisions contain no statutory definition of transgender dressing, leaving the scope of the offence to the enforcing officers.

Malaysian citizens are exposed to both layers simultaneously: the Penal Code sections 377A, 377B and 377D and, for Muslims, the state Sharia enactments carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men.

Residents also face the consequences of raid-based enforcement: in the 28 November 2025 operation 17 civil servants were identified among the 208 detainees and suspended from their jobs. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and with no anti-discrimination statute in force there is no statutory remedy for dismissal or refusal of service on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not address entry or visa screening, airport or immigration inspection of transgender travellers, or the rules on changing sex markers on Malaysian identity documents or passports; those points are unresolved here and are not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, ID document amendments for visitors, and any visitor-facing complaint or consular mechanism beyond the embassy intervention recorded in the 28 November 2025 raid are also not sourced in the material supplied.

Whether the killings documented in 2019, including the Klang case of 25 June 2019, resulted in arrest, prosecution or conviction is unresolved; the documentation available describes police mistreatment and impunity rather than a judicial outcome.

Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 statement about revisiting section 377B produced any legislative or prosecutorial change is not stated in the sources, and the frequency with which section 377B is used against foreign nationals outside venue raids is not quantified.
